title: Phase 7: Redis caching and cache invalidation
description: Implement multi-level Redis caching for policy rules, user dashboard summaries, and organization settings. Apply cache-aside pattern, key versioning, and event-driven invalidation when data changes.

data.text: Caching is the cheapest way to improve throughput — until stale data corrupts user decisions. In an expense platform, a stale policy limit or an outdated approval count could cause compliance violations or duplicate approvals. This phase teaches you what to cache, how long to keep it, and how to evict it safely.

data.title: Candidate cache keys
items: Policy rules: rarely change, expensive to join across categories.
Organization settings: currency, approval chain, per-user feature flags.
User dashboard summary: pending approvals count, recent reports — aggregated from multiple queries.
Department cost center mapping: static for months, referenced in many list queries.

data.caption: Cache layers: application-level Redis + HTTP cache headers for the frontend
data.definition:
graph LR
    C[Client] -->|GET /api/reports/summary| API
    API -->|Check Redis| Redis[(Redis Cache)]
    Redis -->|Hit| API
    API -->|Miss| DB[(SQL Server)]
    DB -->|Hydrate| API
    API -->|SET| Redis
    API -->|200 OK + Cache-Control| C
    subgraph Events
        E1[ExpenseReportSubmitted]
        E2[PolicyRuleUpdated]
        E3[ApprovalGranted]
    end
    E2 -->|Invalidate| Redis

data.text: Never cache forever. Use a version prefix (e.g., `ExpensePlatform:policy:v2`) so you can invalidate all related keys by bumping the version. This is simpler and safer than tracking every individual key.

data.title: C#: ICacheService abstraction with StackExchange.Redis
data.content: The abstraction lets you swap Redis for a no-op implementation in tests.

data.title: C#: Cached policy rule query with versioned key
data.content: Bump the version prefix when all policy rules change (e.g., on Organization update).

data.text: When a PolicyRule is updated, the stale cache entry must die immediately, not on TTL expiry. Publish a PolicyRulesChanged event and let a handler call InvalidateAsync.

data.title: C#: Domain event triggers cache invalidation
data.content: MediatR INotificationHandler responds to domain events.

data.title: Stale cache is worse than no cache
data.text: If a manager approves an expense and the pending-approvals count in Redis doesn't update for 5 minutes, the manager may approve duplicates. Always invalidate on write; use TTL only as a safety net.
React Query (TanStack Query v5) provides client-side caching with stale-while-revalidate semantics. Set cacheTime and gcTime to match the volatility of the data.

data.title: TypeScript: React Query with stale-while-revalidate
data.content: Policy rules rarely change, so a long staleTime is acceptable. Dashboard summaries are short-lived.

items.text: Policy rules cached with versioned key and 30-minute TTL.
PolicyRulesChanged domain event handler invalidates cache on write.
Dashboard summary query uses shorter TTL than policy rules.
Cache hit/miss metrics instrumented with ILogger or OpenTelemetry counters.
Integration test proves stale data is not served after invalidation.

data.title: Phase 7 summary
points: Cache-aside: read-through on miss, explicit write-through on update.
Versioned key prefixes make bulk invalidation a single call.
Domain events are the safest invalidation trigger — they fire after the transaction commits.
Frontend caching complements backend caching; they invalidate independently.
data.takeaway: Caching decisions are about data volatility. Policies are slow-changing; dashboards are fast-changing. Match your TTL and invalidation strategy to the business cost of stale data.
